books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”
Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

stimulus.text: A summary of the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people. In South Carolina, nearly half of white families owned slaves. Most slaveholders owned few enslaved people: about half held fewer than five, and nearly nine in ten held fewer than twenty. Only a small number held more than one hundred.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people, South Carolina 48%, and the distribution of holdings from the census returns. Checked against Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A, which states that the majority of white Southerners owned no slaves.

source: original; data summary from the 1840 United States census
stem: In South Carolina, nearly half of white families owned slaves, far more than in the border states. What does that difference best show?

options.text: Slavery was weakest where cotton farming was strongest, in the Deep South
options.misconception: South Carolina was a cotton state, and slavery was strongest there.

options.text: Border states had larger cotton crops than South Carolina
options.misconception: The Deep South grew the most cotton; border states grew less.

options.text: White families in the Deep South opposed slavery
options.misconception: Nearly half of Deep South families owned slaves, which shows support, not opposition.

options.text: Slaveholding was deepest in the cotton heartland of the Deep South

rationales.A: South Carolina was a cotton state, and slavery was strongest there.
rationales.B: The Deep South grew the most cotton. Border states grew less.
rationales.C: Nearly half of Deep South families owned slaves, which shows support, not opposition.
rationales.D: Where cotton ruled, in South Carolina, nearly half of white families owned slaves, while the border states held far fewer.
rationales.general:
1. Read the figures. Nearly half of white families owned slaves in South Carolina.
2. Ask what the state is. South Carolina was a Deep South cotton state, the heart of the cotton kingdom.
3. Name the pattern. Slaveholding ran deepest where cotton farming ran deepest.
Background: In South Carolina, Black people were also the majority of the population.
Remember: compare the top and the bottom of a range to find what drives it.
